summary: Lists numbers assigned for networks, protocols and related identifiers on the ARPA Internet. Such lists were reissued as assignments changed. This RFC is historic. Replaced by RFC 820.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 790 is a 1981 catalog of numbers used by early Internet protocols. It lists network addresses, protocol identifiers, and service ports, and describes three IPv4 address classes; RFC 820 later replaced it.

questions: class a class b class c networks
subtitle: An early catalog of assigned network, protocol, and port numbers.

tldr.problem: Network protocol implementations needed shared assigned values for identifiers such as network numbers, protocol numbers, ports, and links.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 790 publishes those assigned values, including the three IPv4 address classes and tables of protocols and service ports.
tldr.outcome: RFC 790 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 820.

today: RFC 790 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 820.

sections.title: A Catalog of Assigned Numbers
sections.content: RFC 790 records values assigned to several number series used in network protocol implementations. It covers network, protocol, port or socket, and link numbers, among other assignments. The RFC says the document would be updated periodically and directs people developing protocols or applications that need assignments to contact the person managing them.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is a reference list of numbers that protocols and services use. Its purpose is to help implementations use assigned values consistently.

sections.title: Three IPv4 Address Classes
sections.content:
The RFC describes a 32-bit Internet Protocol address divided into a network part and a local-address part. Class A uses a 7-bit network number and a 24-bit local address, allowing 128 networks. Class B uses 14 network bits and 16 local bits, allowing 16,384 networks. Class C uses 21 network bits and 8 local bits, allowing 2,097,152 networks.

The first bits of the address identify its class. The RFC also shows a dotted decimal notation that divides the address into four 8-bit fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo groups IPv4 addresses into three classes with different amounts of space for network and local addresses. The first bits show which class an address uses.

sections.title: Protocol and Service Numbers
sections.content:
The RFC lists Internet version numbers and protocol numbers. The IP Protocol field is described as 8 bits; the list assigns 6 to TCP and 17 to User Datagram Protocol. It also lists port or socket assignments for services, including Telnet, SMTP, and Trivial File Transfer.

These are historical entries in the assigned-number catalog, not guidance about present-day deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: Tables connect numeric identifiers to protocols and services. A system can use the assigned number to identify what protocol or service a value refers to.

references.text: Postel, J., ed., "Internet Protocol - DARPA Internet Program Protocol Specification", RFC 791, September 1981.
